name: Question 19
problem:
Consider a function $d(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{d(t)}=D(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-9t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $D(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t=D(s+9),
$$

where 

$$
s+9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-9.
$$

Question 19

Consider a function d(t) such that its Laplace transform is L{d(t)}=D(s) for s>s0. Suppose we wish to find L{e−9td(t)}. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

e−st⋅e−9td(t)
est⋅e9td(t)
e−st⋅e−9td(t)
est⋅e−9td(t)
e−st⋅e9td(t)
e−(s+9)t
e−(s−9)t
e(s+9)t
e(s−9)t
e−(s+9)t
D(s+9)
D(s)
D(s−9)
D(s+9)
s>s0−9
s>s0−9
s>s0
s>s0+9
L{e−9td(t)}=∫0∞{(est⋅e9td(t))(S0)}dt=∫0∞{(e−(s−9)t)(S1)}d(t)dt={(D(s))(S2)}for{(s>s0−9)(S3)}.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

L{e−9td(t)}=∫0∞e−st⋅e−9td(t)dt=∫0∞e−(s+9)td(t)dt

Now, recall that D(s)=∫0∞e−std(t)dt, where s>s0. Therefore, ∫0∞e−(s+9)td(t)dt=D(s+9), where s+9>s0⇒s>s0−9.
